chunks: It has been narrated that al-Bahira is the female camel when she has produced five offspring; if the fifth was a male, they would slaughter him and men and women would eat from him.
And if the fifth was a female, they would slit her ear, meaning they cut it, and her flesh and milk would be forbidden for women and men.
And if she died naturally, she would be allowed for women.
Al-Sa'iba is the camel that walks freely due to an oath that is upon a man if Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, saves him from an illness or makes him reach his home, that he would do that.
Al-Waseela from the sheep is a sheep that gives birth to seven offspring; if the seventh was a male, he would be slaughtered, and men and women would eat from him.
And if it was a female, it would be left among the sheep.

And if it was a male and a female, they said: 'It has connected with its brother,' so it would not be slaughtered, and its flesh would be forbidden for women, except if something dies from it, and so it would then be allowed to eat for men and women.
Al-Ham is the male stud when he rides and produces his son; they would say: 'His back is heated.'
It may be narrated that al-Ham is the camel that has produced ten offspring, due to which they would say: 'His back is heated,' and so it would not be ridden, nor prevented from care nor water.

key_terms.السَّائِبَة: A camel released freely due to a vow if the owner survived illness or journey
key_terms.الْبَحِيرَة: A female camel whose offspring were exempted from work or slaughter
key_terms.الْحَام: A male stud camel or camel with many offspring, considered 'heated' and exempt
key_terms.الْوَصِيلَة: A sheep whose seventh offspring was considered connected/sacred

ai.seo_question: What were the pre-Islamic customs regarding Bahira, Sa'iba, Waseela, and Ham animals?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq details the specific criteria for al-Bahira, al-Sa'iba, al-Waseela, and al-Ham, illustrating how pre-Islamic Arabs designated animals as sacred or exempt from labor based on their offspring's gender and count. This narration provides the historical backdrop for the Quranic critique of these arbitrary customs, emphasizing their lack of divine basis and their role in distinguishing between permissible and forbidden provisions through human whim rather than revelation.

en.basel-kadem: It has been narrated that baheera is the female camel when having produced five bellies, and if the fifth was a male, they would slaughter it and it would be eaten by men and women,
and if the fifth was a female, they slit  its ear, meaning that they cut it, and its flesh and milk would be forbidden for women and men,
and if it [1] died (naturally), it would be allowed for women.
The sa’iba is the male camel that walks freely due to an oath that is upon a man if Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, saves him from an illness or makes him reach his home.
The waseela from sheep is a sheep that would give birth to seven bellies. If the seventh was a male, he would be slaughtered, and men and women would eat from him,
and if it was a female, it would be left among the sheep,

and if it a male and a female, they said: «It has connected  with its brother» and it would not be slaughtered, and its flesh would be forbidden for women, except if something dies from it, and so, it would then be allowed to eat for men and women.
The haam is the male when a boy rides his sons. They would say: «His back is heated» .
It may be narrated that the haam is the camel that has produced ten bellies, due to which they would say: «His back is heated» and so it would not be ridden, nor prevented from care nor water.
